sources.title: Kaw Nation: History of Kaw Nation
sources.note: Official identity and migration account, opening paragraphs; reservoir displacement. Broad chronology is approximate. Do not adopt its later suggestion that agriculture first arrived through American pressure: Kanza farming long preceded these policies.

sources.title: Kaw Nation: The Kanza People
sources.note: Mid-eighteenth-century regional strength, hunting territory and 1825 land reduction. Page conflates the 1872 removal act with actual relocation; the card uses 1873 from the Chapman Center and 2025 tribal newsletter.

sources.title: Kansas Historical Society: Fool Chief’s Village
sources.note: Direct extraction returns navigation only; full indexed original checked with query site.kansashistory.gov "Fool Chief" "30" "seasonal". Seasonal calendar, bark houses, central hearth, bunks and hide trade.

sources.title: Kansas State University Chapman Center: Treaty of 1846, annotated text
sources.note: Introduction and annotations to Articles 1, 2 and 5; same text also at kansastreaties.ccrsdigitalprojects.com. Floods, land cession, government obligations and 1873 removal. Count as one document.

sources.title: Kansas Historical Society: Kaw Mission
sources.note: Indexed original contains school opening, dormitories, subjects, attendance limits and 1854 closure. Distinguish teaching agriculture from introducing agriculture.

sources.title: Kaw Nation: Self-Governance at a Glance
sources.note: Official program explanation and specific Kaw dates: IHS 1995, BIA 1996. Federal program administration, not newly invented sovereignty.

sources.title: Kaw Nation: Kanza Language
sources.note: Names Kaw/Kansa/Kanza and Dhegiha linguistic relationships; current courses, vocabulary and family camping materials. Related peoples remain distinct.

sources.title: Kaw Nation: Language for Families and Communities
sources.note: Direct PDF text, PDF page 2 (zero-based index 1), General conversation phrases: Nompéaⁿhi. / I’m hungry. Following page explains positional continuatives. Screenshot fetch failed; no visual inspection claimed. Later grammar section has an obvious hungry/sick typo not used.

sources.title: Kanza News, April 2025: Kaw Nation Language Department’s award-winning short film
sources.note: Printed page 8, PDF index 7. Actual 1873 removal separated from congressional legislation, named student actors and elders, director Dylan Bellmard. Unrelated caption’s 1808 flood not used.

sources.title: Kaw Nation: Kanza Museum
sources.note: Current exhibition description accessed September 2026; five audio sections, documents, treaty reproductions, drawers and clan book. Does not imply every document is an original artifact.

sources.title: Kaw Nation: Historical Events
sources.note: Selected early-1970s paragraph: cemetery moved to Newkirk, council house and Washunga residents relocated for Kaw Lake. No disputed dam-completion year adopted.

sources.title: Thomas P. Myers: Birth and Rebirth of the Omaha, University of Nebraska State Museum, 1992
sources.note: Exhibition developed in cooperation with the Omaha Tribe. Origins, clan organization and 1989 Sacred Pole return. Migration chronology remains broad; archaeological attribution to Angel/Caborn-Welborn is explicitly conditional and not asserted in card.

sources.title: National Park Service: Omaha Big Village
sources.note: Modern site account and 1804 Ordway quotation distinguish estimates. Card avoids conflicting epidemic fractions and exact founding date, using late-eighteenth-century village, Fort Charles 1795 and epidemic around 1800.

sources.title: James Owen Dorsey: Omaha Dwellings, Furniture, and Implements, 1896
sources.note: Primary ethnographic report, fieldwork from 1878. Printed pp. 269 to 270 earth lodges, 276 brooms, 276 to 277 mortars. Same work directly read at https://www.gutenberg.org/files/19913/19913-h/19913-h.htm; both access copies treated as one source. No claim of unchanged prehistoric customs.

sources.title: Treaty with the Omaha, 1854: Oklahoma State University treaty transcription
sources.note: Primary Articles 1 and 4; cession south of a specified line west of Missouri and reserved homeland. Do not adopt the inaccurate blanket claim that all western Missouri lands were ceded.

sources.title: National Park Service: Susan La Flesche Picotte
sources.note: Medical education, first in class, return to reservation and house calls with children. Page has errors: Hampton is not in New Jersey; husband died in 1905 and could not personally help open hospital in 1913. Those claims excluded; hospital facts from nomination.

sources.title: National Park Service: Dr. Susan LaFlesche Picotte Memorial Hospital, landmark nomination
sources.note: Printed page 11 (PDF index 10): separate towels/basins, meals, school fountains and examinations. Printed pp. 12 to 13: January 1913 opening, wards and bathrooms. No present-day treatment advice.

sources.title: National Park Service: Susan La Flesche Picotte House
sources.note: Diary evidence of interpreting wills and unpaid rent; March 2, 1911 meeting of more than 60 Omaha about inheritance rights. House completed 1907, a detail not needed in card.

sources.title: Library of Congress: Omaha Indian Music, album introduction
sources.note: Fletcher-La Flesche cylinder collection discussion: probably La Flesche recorded most; 1895 first reservation use and 90 cylinders over following decade. No song lyrics reproduced.

sources.title: Omaha Tribe of Nebraska and Iowa: Against the Current, October 2024
sources.note: Direct PDF text, p. 1 / index 0 pairs Táxti kigthígthoⁿi-kʰe with When the Deer Rut. Page 2 / index 1 language department emphasizes daily use and describes staged plans rather than completed targets. Screenshot attempt timed out; no visual inspection claimed.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: Shared narrative for two imported Kaw/Kansa homeland labels; not shared with related Osage, Omaha, Ponca or Quapaw.
batchIdentityNotes.mapEvidence: kansa index 1530 to 1783; world-1530 polygon bbox [-97.8076,38.2935,-94.4739,40.2490]. washtage-monzhan-kaw-kansa index 1492 to 1500; world-1492 broader Kansas-region polygon bbox [-100.6372,37.0277,-94.3947,40.3290]. Original intervals retained.
batchIdentityNotes.limitations: Kaw Nation explicitly equates Kaw, Kansa and Kanza. No claim that the unverified imported Washtáge Moⁿzháⁿ phrase is translated by the card. The early polygons are not securely dated borders: official migration account gives a broad sixteenth- to eighteenth-century interval. Public opening warns explicitly. Modern Oklahoma phase is clearly separated. Unreliable dates on the general Kanza Timeline page excluded.

batchIdentityNotes.decision: Shared Omaha people narrative for English and Umoⁿhoⁿ labels; no Ponca or other related people absorbed.
batchIdentityNotes.mapEvidence: omaha index 1530 to 1783; world-1530 polygon bbox [-98.2936,41.1922,-96.0976,42.9034]. umonhon-omaha index 1492 to 1500; world-1492 polygon bbox [-98.3944,41.1460,-95.7340,42.8603]. Both locate a Nebraska/Missouri River homeland; distinct original intervals retained.
batchIdentityNotes.limitations: October 2024 official newsletter names both Omaha and Umoⁿhoⁿ. Museum origins account places migration over a broad interval and northern Iowa presence by 1697, so an exact 1492 or 1530 Nebraska outline is not established. Public opening makes this limitation visible. The conditional Angel-site ancestry hypothesis is not adopted. Household accounts are expressly nineteenth-century documentation, not assigned invented early item dates.
